[POC_SCOPE.md](../POC_SCOPE.md) records the local setup and remaining reviewer checks; the hosted design below remains the broader v1 roadmap. ## State **clanker v1 is a hosted Hermes-based Slack assistant for general browser tasks and access management. Reuse Hermes first; focus clanker-specific work on routing and authorization, and add code only for demonstrated gaps.** The repository contains this scope, a verification strategy and source review, plus a pinned stock Hermes local baseline and clanker Slack setup files. The local CLI starts, 47 targeted upstream routing/session tests pass, and real Slack owner commands work in a DM and the test channel; see [LOCAL_BASELINE.md](../verification/LOCAL_BASELINE.md). The full Slack/browser E2E, deployed reviewer experience, and v1 acceptance remain open. Upstream documentation and synthetic tests establish narrower capabilities, not that our chosen deployment has passed its requirements. **Selected browser architecture:** each assigned worker VM runs Hermes and local Chromium, controlled through Hermes's existing Browser Use driver. This is the selected v1 design; the VM pool, browser workflow, and persistence across VM replacement still require implementation and verification. **Selected access interface:** a hosted clanker vault web app uses Sign in with Slack to collect and manage saved access. Reuse Hermes's vault implementation and UI/API components behind clanker's authenticated owner and task checks. This integration is selected, not implemented or verified. The assignment permits third-party components and prioritizes a smooth working experience over code volume. A successful v1 may consist mostly of configuration, deployment, integration fixes, and verification. The user reported that Sahan approved Slack identity replacing the assignment's Google-only chatbot sign-in requirement. Reviewers still use Slack without their own model-provider accounts. This is the preferred setup to evaluate, not a verified funding arrangement. [Hermes documents](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/integrations/providers) device-code authorization, which lets the owner approve login in their browser while Hermes runs and stores its authentication on the cloud host. [OpenAI documents](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001542-using-your-chatgpt-plan-in-other-apps-and-sites) eligible plan usage in supported integrations; Hermes's exact account eligibility and quota accounting remain unverified for this deployment. Verify authentication refresh and persistence across a cloud restart with the owner's laptop out of the execution path. Subscription-funded inference does not establish coverage for hosting or separately billed browser/tool services. Record those costs separately. Any alternative paid inference setup remains a separate decision if the preferred route cannot meet the requirements. ## Reuse from Hermes Pin the Hermes version and required integrations, configure them, and verify their behavior in the deployed Slack experience. | Capability | Starting point | What clanker must establish | | --- | --- | --- | | Agent harness | Hermes's agent loop, tools, skills, and session machinery | General tasks work with the selected model and enabled tools. | | Slack interface | Hermes's existing Slack adapter and gateway | App configuration, authenticated admission, correct conversation routing, and replies. | | Browser automation | Local Chromium inside the assigned worker VM, controlled by Hermes's existing Browser Use driver (`browser_exec`) | Background browser work, uploads/downloads, secure login/handoff, scoped browser persistence, and saved-access reuse across worker replacement. | | Credentials and 2FA | Hermes's credential vault, Desktop vault form/API components, protected browser filling, TOTP support, and access-management controls | The hosted clanker vault web app authenticates with Slack and enforces owner/task/site access before saving or using credentials. Reviewers can securely provide, reuse, and remove access. Resolve the TOTP choice below. | | Profiles and conversations | Existing profile routing, DM/channel/thread sessions, memory, and persistence | The selected configuration enforces the intended tenant, owner, and audience boundaries across turns and restarts. | Start from the documented [browser integration](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/), [credential vault](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/credential-vault/), [profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes), and [session behavior](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions). Native vault UI/API components cover CLI/Desktop use; the selected hosted web app adds the Slack identity and access-request authorization boundary. The complete collection, reuse, and revocation flow still needs validation. ## Architecture and routing contract **Use a shared Slack gateway and a pool of isolated Hermes worker VMs.** The gateway binds authenticated tenant, sender, and conversation audience to an authorized profile before queueing the task. The scheduler assigns a ready VM to that private or shared context; the VM pool manager maintains clean warm spares, adds capacity within limits, and removes excess idle capacity. Each worker runs Hermes, its Browser Use driver, and local Chromium inside the same VM. Profiles and permitted browser/file state persist beyond the worker's lifetime. The hosting provider, pool sizes, idle timeout, and storage implementation remain open choices. ```mermaid flowchart TD Slack["Slack workspaces

item.stdout:
# Vault invitations and requester authorization

The vault has one **Invite to vault** button. The owner chooses a current Slack
member, checks which saved logins, API keys and payment cards to share, then
confirms use of only that selection on their behalf. Nothing is checked for a
new member, and credentials added later stay private. **People with access**
groups each member's shared credentials; **Edit access** reopens the checklist
with that member's existing selection, and **Remove** revokes their access.
The member sees **Shared with you** in their vault. An
invitation takes effect immediately; it does not send an external Slack message.
The saved credential remains in the owner's encrypted native vault. The guest
receives a grant handle and metadata, not a copied vault entry.

This implements explicit delegation. It does **not** establish that the reported
Gmail disclosure is fixed in the running system. The gateway has not been
reloaded, no real invitation has been created, and the consumer browser
provider's isolation and cookie-deletion behavior remain unverified.

## Permission boundary

Slack OIDC establishes the owner of the vault web session. Owner and workspace
come from that session, never request-body fields. CSRF and exact-origin checks
cover invite and revoke. Only native items in that owner's vault can be invited;
guests cannot pass an invited handle to create another invitation.

A durable grant binds workspace, owner, recipient and selected credential.
Saving a member's checklist validates the entire selection and applies all
permission additions/removals in one database transaction. Invalid or foreign
items cause no partial changes. Still-selected credentials retain their grant
handles; unchecked credentials and their pending approvals are revoked before
browser cleanup. Selecting credentials grants no wildcard access to the vault.
Its identity binding includes kind, origin, account identifier and creation
time. The runtime resolves that grant for the authenticated requesting member,
checks current membership of both parties, and verifies the selected native item
still exists with that binding. An unrelated native handle, another member's
grant, a removed or changed account, or a disabled member is denied. Reinvitation
after revocation produces a new grant handle.

These are credential-use permissions. A login can provide the full website
account access available to that login; an API key can provide the permissions
the service gives that key. The implementation does not impose a new read-only
role inside either service. Preventing onward grants is an application rule;
it is not a guarantee that an authorized recipient cannot copy account data or
that a third-party browser provider cannot access an entered credential.

## Execution

Logins fill the requester's supervised local browser, after exact origin and
supported-field inspection. The selected owner password is supplied by the
trusted backend, without switching the active Hermes home to the owner. Owner
TOTP or a hosted owner-only code form can satisfy verification. The one-use code
is consumed in the original requester's task, and automatic resume retains that
requester's source, home and DM.

API requests use `clanker_api_request`: the backend adds the owned or invited key
to a supported authentication header. Calls accept relative paths on the saved
HTTPS origin, reject authentication/Host/Cookie overrides, reject private or
local DNS addresses, pin the connection to a resolved public IP, and verify TLS
against the original hostname. Redirects do not forward authentication. Request
and response sizes are limited. Key values are registered for redaction and
scrubbed from responses. Synthetic transport tests verify these restrictions;
no real external API operation was performed for this change.

Cards use only the requester's supervised local checkout. An invitation lets
the member request a purchase; each exact purchase still needs the **card
owner's** hosted approval and current CVV. The owner sees merchant, order, total,
checkout text and requester. Approval does not transfer the task to the owner.
The handler rechecks the original browser, task, conversation and checkout,
consumes approval and CVV before fill/submission, and refuses replay. Submitted
is not paid; the merchant receipt must be checked. Unsupported payment frames,
wallets, subscriptions and bank approval retain their existing limits.

## Revocation and cookies

Revocation is committed before cleanup and cancels pending delegated code/card
approvals. Secret-bearing browser use is recorded before handoff, with an atomic
active-grant check. This covers a revoke racing between handle resolution and
the usage record. Work already in flight may finish before interruption; the
implementation cannot undo earlier disclosures or completed external actions.

For local Chromium, revoke interrupts the original requester task, closes their
private browsers and deletes their Chromium cookie profile under the guest
execution lock. Cleanup conservatively removes all of that recipient's private
browser state, including sessions used for other valid grants. It preserves the
owner's browser and native vault. An active grant can be used again in a fresh
guest browser after cleanup. API requests have no reusable browser cookies.

If cleanup fails, the grant remains revoked and the recorded usage keeps future
browser/terminal execution blocked. The web UI shows **cleanup pending** and
offers retry. **People with access** also exposes orphan invitations whose
native credential was removed, so that member's access can still be removed or
cleanup retried.

Consumer Browser Tool exposes task stop but no reviewed cookie/session deletion
operation. Its stop result now reports `profile_retained: null` (unknown),
correcting the previous unsupported claim of cookie deletion. A required purge
stops the task, keeps a blocked tombstone, and returns cleanup pending. Repeated
stop/retry does not clear that block. Operator cleanup needs an actual provider
deletion/reconciliation capability before a verified reset can be recorded;
this implementation does not supply that capability.

## Browser routing and unresolved incident work

New cloud state keys include workspace, authenticated requester and resolved
home, independent of the short session name or a shared conversation profile.
State carries an explicit owner marker. Provider session IDs are recorded with
that owner/context, and a recorded collision is refused and quarantined. Legacy
state is not silently adopted by the new namespace. Unknown dispatch outcomes
retain their retry block.

These controls govern Clanker's assignments and known grants. They do not prove
a fresh remote browser lacks another account's pre-existing cookies. Provider
ownership collisions are detected on acknowledgement, after task dispatch;
that check cannot undo observations the provider made before acknowledging.
Free-form remote task instructions are not an account-authorization boundary.
The reported disclosure therefore still requires tracing and invalidating
affected legacy/provider state, a provider-enforced requester isolation and
pre-read authorization design, and real two-requester/DM-handoff acceptance.
Existing login state alone must never be used as permission.

## Verified locally

The canonical Hermes test runner passed **79 tests across five affected files**:
invitations, vault, payments, consumer Browser Tool and managed cloud browser.
Coverage includes all three credential kinds, owner/recipient/workspace checks,
CSRF and forged identity fields, persistence, onward-sharing denial, revoked
access, cleanup failure, same session names/shared profile names, recorded
provider-session collisions, delegated code and payment resume, origin-bound
API requests, TLS/DNS pinning and redirect rejection. Checklist coverage adds
multi-credential sharing, atomic rejection without partial permission changes,
stable handles for retained credentials, revocation of unchecked items, no
automatic sharing of later credentials, and removal of an inactive member.

The actual sandboxed Chromium probe exercised A → B → A with two disposable
homes: owner login, denial of the owner's raw handle to the guest, invited login
fill, owner-only HTTP approval, one guest dummy checkout with an observed dummy
receipt, payment replay denial, CVV consumption, no copied guest vault entry,
guest cookie-profile removal when the login is unchecked in that member's
selection, and preservation of the owner's browser.
The same guest task/session can start a fresh browser after cleanup, while the
revoked login remains denied and an unrelated active card grant remains listed.
Its receipt is
[`2026-10-06-invitation-local-browser.json`](../../verification/evidence/2026-10-06-invitation-local-browser.json).

The visible UI check uses disposable identities and dummy credentials on
loopback. The owner initially selected login and API key; the guest saw those
two entries and no card. Edit access restored that checklist; unchecking the
login and checking the card made guest reload show only API key and card, with
the per-purchase owner-approval label. Desktop and mobile checklists and the
member-level sharing list were visually checked. Removing the member through
the single member row then made guest reload show no saved or invited access.
Screenshots are saved as
`output/playwright/vault-invite-selection-desktop.png`,
`vault-edit-selection-mobile.png` and `vault-sharing-members-mobile.png`.
Earlier per-credential Invite
screenshots represent the superseded design. The missing favicon is unrelated
to invitation behavior.
No mailbox content, real credential, live Slack message, real card
charge or production configuration change is used as verification evidence.
# Owner-approved payment cards in the local POC

Clanker can collect a card in the private vault form, save the reusable number,
expiry and optional cardholder name, and use it in a particular checkout after
the owner approves that purchase. This implementation is local POC code. Real
merchant payment acceptance, production hosting and payment compliance have not
been verified.

## Flow

1. Prepare a one-time card checkout with `browser_exec` in the owner's private
   local browser. `clanker_request_payment` takes its exact `checkout_url`, the
   merchant, item/quantity/delivery summary, final `amount_minor` including fees,
   currency, and an optional saved-card handle.
2. The backend checks that the browser endpoint belongs to that profile, finds
   the exact checkout tab, and captures its origin, URL, visible contents and one
   visible Pay/Place order button. A recognizable final-total line must match
   the requested amount. Unsupported or ambiguous totals fail before collection.
3. The existing private Slack handoff sends an owner-bound vault link. The same
   Slack OIDC session and CSRF controls protect the form. The owner sees the
   merchant, origin, summary, amount and expandable actual checkout text. Card
   fields are masked. Approval is explicit and specific to one purchase.
4. Saving encrypts reusable card fields in the owner's native Hermes VaultStore.
   CVV is excluded from that item. It is separately encrypted for this approval,
   expires within five minutes, and is cleared on use, cancellation or expiry
   cleanup. Saved-card reuse shows the last four digits and asks for current CVV
   and fresh approval. The approval link expires after fifteen minutes.
5. The task resumes with a request ID, never card values. `clanker_pay` verifies
   owner, profile, task, conversation, exact browser, page contents and stamped
   button. It consumes approval durably before card-bearing browser I/O, rechecks
   the checkout in the same JavaScript operation that fills and clicks, and
   returns `submitted`. The merchant receipt must establish payment success.
   Unknown outcomes cannot replay that approval and require reconciliation.

## Supported scope and trust

- Cards and approvals are tied to the exact checkout origin. Current currencies
  are INR, USD, EUR, GBP, CAD and AUD, all with two minor-unit decimal places.
  The final-total parser is deliberately conservative; it does not claim
  compatibility with any particular real merchant's checkout layout.

  button. Hosted payment iframes, wallets, subscriptions and automatic bank/3DS
  completion are not implemented. Bank approval requires owner action.
- Card data is delivered directly over the owned local CDP WebSocket, not through
  a cloud browser task, model tool arguments, Slack, process argv or environment.
  Cloud Browser Tool cards are refused because that provider can log request
  payloads. Login routing prefers the local supervisor when one is active.
- The guarded card release and one-use approval rules are enforced by the
  dedicated payment handlers. Generic browser code is still capable of clicking
  a merchant-saved payment method; instructions prohibit doing that. This is
  not an enforcement boundary against arbitrary malicious agent code or a
  compromised merchant. Browser inspection is not proof of what a merchant's
  backend will charge.
- The gateway/operator host remains trusted. Encryption keys are local beside
  encrypted data. Existing host access, generated-code and profile-isolation
  limitations remain relevant. Temporary encrypted CVV deletion is logical
  cleanup, not a claim of forensic erasure across backups or disk snapshots.
- Removing a card cancels pending owner requests through the existing disconnect
  flow. A saved-card approval validates that the handle still exists and belongs
  to the owner on the captured origin.

## Verification

The canonical Hermes runner passed 117 distinct tests across the payment, hosted-vault,
Browser Tool, cloud browser, native store and native browser-vault suites. The
payment suite covers A → B → A HTTP approval/storage/resume, wrong owner, CSRF,
link replay, expiry, cancellation, changed checkout, wrong task/thread, uncertain
submission and mismatched final totals. The initial six-file run passed 116;
after adding the resumed-purchase `/stop` cancellation case, the two affected
suites passed all 40 tests. Cancellation revokes the temporary CVV before card
release even after the approval has resumed its task.

`verification/probes/clanker_payment_browser_probe.py` passed seven checks with
real sandboxed Chromium and dummy cards: tool discovery and owned endpoint,
first-card submission and receipt, saved-card reuse after fresh HTTP approval,
CVV cleanup, changed-cart refusal, a checkout change between inspection and
write, and foreign-profile refusal. The controlled Example.com DOM replaces the
checkout and generates local dummy receipts. No payment network or real Slack
message is used. Receipt: `verification/evidence/2026-10-06-payment-local-browser.json`.

The local UI fixture at port 8769 shows the actual form and confirmation code.
Approval cleared all inputs and link fragments, hid the form and displayed
Purchase approved. Decline displayed Purchase declined and cleared the form.
Screenshots are under `output/playwright/clanker-payment-*`.

Fresh plugin discovery is verified in temporary profiles. The currently running
Slack gateway predates these handlers; activating them requires a reload after
its active work is accounted for. No live Slack purchase has been performed.

## Files

Implementation: `runtime/vault/payments.py`, the existing vault HTTP/form assets,
and `runtime/seatbelt/plugin.py`. The minimal native store change makes CVV
optional for reusable payment items. Its patch and corresponding native test
are in `patches/hermes/payment-vault.patch`, included by
`scripts/apply-hermes-mods` after the API-key patch.

# Vault invitations and requester authorization

The vault has one **Invite to vault** button. The owner chooses a current Slack
member, checks which saved logins, API keys and payment cards to share, then
confirms use of only that selection on their behalf. Nothing is checked for a
new member, and credentials added later stay private. **People with access**
groups each member's shared credentials; **Edit access** reopens the checklist
with that member's existing selection, and **Remove** revokes their access.
The member sees **Shared with you** in their vault. An
invitation takes effect immediately; it does not send an external Slack message.
The saved credential remains in the owner's encrypted native vault. The guest
receives a grant handle and metadata, not a copied vault entry.

This implements explicit delegation. It does **not** establish that the reported
Gmail disclosure is fixed in the running system. The gateway has not been
reloaded, no real invitation has been created, and the consumer browser
provider's isolation and cookie-deletion behavior remain unverified.

## Permission boundary

Slack OIDC establishes the owner of the vault web session. Owner and workspace
come from that session, never request-body fields. CSRF and exact-origin checks
cover invite and revoke. Only native items in that owner's vault can be invited;
guests cannot pass an invited handle to create another invitation.

A durable grant binds workspace, owner, recipient and selected credential.
Saving a member's checklist validates the entire selection and applies all
permission additions/removals in one database transaction. Invalid or foreign
items cause no partial changes. Still-selected credentials retain their grant
handles; unchecked credentials and their pending approvals are revoked before
browser cleanup. Selecting credentials grants no wildcard access to the vault.
Its identity binding includes kind, origin, account identifier and creation
time. The runtime resolves that grant for the authenticated requesting member,
checks current membership of both parties, and verifies the selected native item
still exists with that binding. An unrelated native handle, another member's
grant, a removed or changed account, or a disabled member is denied. Reinvitation
after revocation produces a new grant handle.

These are credential-use permissions. A login can provide the full website
account access available to that login; an API key can provide the permissions
the service gives that key. The implementation does not impose a new read-only
role inside either service. Preventing onward grants is an application rule;
it is not a guarantee that an authorized recipient cannot copy account data or
that a third-party browser provider cannot access an entered credential.

## Execution

Logins fill the requester's supervised local browser, after exact origin and
supported-field inspection. The selected owner password is supplied by the
trusted backend, without switching the active Hermes home to the owner. Owner
TOTP or a hosted owner-only code form can satisfy verification. The one-use code
is consumed in the original requester's task, and automatic resume retains that
requester's source, home and DM.

API requests use `clanker_api_request`: the backend adds the owned or invited key
to a supported authentication header. Calls accept relative paths on the saved
HTTPS origin, reject authentication/Host/Cookie overrides, reject private or
local DNS addresses, pin the connection to a resolved public IP, and verify TLS
against the original hostname. Redirects do not forward authentication. Request
and response sizes are limited. Key values are registered for redaction and
scrubbed from responses. Synthetic transport tests verify these restrictions;
no real external API operation was performed for this change.

Cards use only the requester's supervised local checkout. An invitation lets
the member request a purchase; each exact purchase still needs the **card
owner's** hosted approval and current CVV. The owner sees merchant, order, total,
checkout text and requester. Approval does not transfer the task to the owner.
The handler rechecks the original browser, task, conversation and checkout,
consumes approval and CVV before fill/submission, and refuses replay. Submitted
is not paid; the merchant receipt must be checked. Unsupported payment frames,
wallets, subscriptions and bank approval retain their existing limits.

## Revocation and cookies

Revocation is committed before cleanup and cancels pending delegated code/card
approvals. Secret-bearing browser use is recorded before handoff, with an atomic
active-grant check. This covers a revoke racing between handle resolution and
the usage record. Work already in flight may finish before interruption; the
implementation cannot undo earlier disclosures or completed external actions.

For local Chromium, revoke interrupts the original requester task, closes their
private browsers and deletes their Chromium cookie profile under the guest
execution lock. Cleanup conservatively removes all of that recipient's private
browser state, including sessions used for other valid grants. It preserves the
owner's browser and native vault. An active grant can be used again in a fresh
guest browser after cleanup. API requests have no reusable browser cookies.

If cleanup fails, the grant remains revoked and the recorded usage keeps future
browser/terminal execution blocked. The web UI shows **cleanup pending** and
offers retry. **People with access** also exposes orphan invitations whose
native credential was removed, so that member's access can still be removed or
cleanup retried.

Consumer Browser Tool exposes task stop but no reviewed cookie/session deletion
operation. Its stop result now reports `profile_retained: null` (unknown),
correcting the previous unsupported claim of cookie deletion. A required purge
stops the task, keeps a blocked tombstone, and returns cleanup pending. Repeated
stop/retry does not clear that block. Operator cleanup needs an actual provider
deletion/reconciliation capability before a verified reset can be recorded;
this implementation does not supply that capability.

## Browser routing and unresolved incident work

New cloud state keys include workspace, authenticated requester and resolved
home, independent of the short session name or a shared conversation profile.
State carries an explicit owner marker. Provider session IDs are recorded with
that owner/context, and a recorded collision is refused and quarantined. Legacy
state is not silently adopted by the new namespace. Unknown dispatch outcomes
retain their retry block.

These controls govern Clanker's assignments and known grants. They do not prove
a fresh remote browser lacks another account's pre-existing cookies. Provider
ownership collisions are detected on acknowledgement, after task dispatch;
that check cannot undo observations the provider made before acknowledging.
Free-form remote task instructions are not an account-authorization boundary.
The reported disclosure therefore still requires tracing and invalidating
affected legacy/provider state, a provider-enforced requester isolation and
pre-read authorization design, and real two-requester/DM-handoff acceptance.
Existing login state alone must never be used as permission.

## Verified locally

The canonical Hermes test runner passed **79 tests across five affected files**:
invitations, vault, payments, consumer Browser Tool and managed cloud browser.
Coverage includes all three credential kinds, owner/recipient/workspace checks,
CSRF and forged identity fields, persistence, onward-sharing denial, revoked
access, cleanup failure, same session names/shared profile names, recorded
provider-session collisions, delegated code and payment resume, origin-bound
API requests, TLS/DNS pinning and redirect rejection. Checklist coverage adds
multi-credential sharing, atomic rejection without partial permission changes,
stable handles for retained credentials, revocation of unchecked items, no
automatic sharing of later credentials, and removal of an inactive member.

The actual sandboxed Chromium probe exercised A → B → A with two disposable
homes: owner login, denial of the owner's raw handle to the guest, invited login
fill, owner-only HTTP approval, one guest dummy checkout with an observed dummy
receipt, payment replay denial, CVV consumption, no copied guest vault entry,
guest cookie-profile removal when the login is unchecked in that member's
selection, and preservation of the owner's browser.
The same guest task/session can start a fresh browser after cleanup, while the
revoked login remains denied and an unrelated active card grant remains listed.
Its receipt is
[`2026-10-06-invitation-local-browser.json`](../../verification/evidence/2026-10-06-invitation-local-browser.json).

The visible UI check uses disposable identities and dummy credentials on
loopback. The owner initially selected login and API key; the guest saw those
two entries and no card. Edit access restored that checklist; unchecking the
login and checking the card made guest reload show only API key and card, with
the per-purchase owner-approval label. Desktop and mobile checklists and the
member-level sharing list were visually checked. Removing the member through
the single member row then made guest reload show no saved or invited access.
Screenshots are saved as
`output/playwright/vault-invite-selection-desktop.png`,
`vault-edit-selection-mobile.png` and `vault-sharing-members-mobile.png`.
Earlier per-credential Invite
screenshots represent the superseded design. The missing favicon is unrelated
to invitation behavior.
No mailbox content, real credential, live Slack message, real card
charge or production configuration change is used as verification evidence.
# Owner-approved payment cards in the local POC

Clanker can collect a card in the private vault form, save the reusable number,
expiry and optional cardholder name, and use it in a particular checkout after
the owner approves that purchase. This implementation is local POC code. Real
merchant payment acceptance, production hosting and payment compliance have not
been verified.

## Flow

1. Prepare a one-time card checkout with `browser_exec` in the owner's private
   local browser. `clanker_request_payment` takes its exact `checkout_url`, the
   merchant, item/quantity/delivery summary, final `amount_minor` including fees,
   currency, and an optional saved-card handle.
2. The backend checks that the browser endpoint belongs to that profile, finds
   the exact checkout tab, and captures its origin, URL, visible contents and one
   visible Pay/Place order button. A recognizable final-total line must match
   the requested amount. Unsupported or ambiguous totals fail before collection.
3. The existing private Slack handoff sends an owner-bound vault link. The same
   Slack OIDC session and CSRF controls protect the form. The owner sees the
   merchant, origin, summary, amount and expandable actual checkout text. Card
   fields are masked. Approval is explicit and specific to one purchase.
4. Saving encrypts reusable card fields in the owner's native Hermes VaultStore.
   CVV is excluded from that item. It is separately encrypted for this approval,
   expires within five minutes, and is cleared on use, cancellation or expiry
   cleanup. Saved-card reuse shows the last four digits and asks for current CVV
   and fresh approval. The approval link expires after fifteen minutes.
5. The task resumes with a request ID, never card values. `clanker_pay` verifies
   owner, profile, task, conversation, exact browser, page contents and stamped
   button. It consumes approval durably before card-bearing browser I/O, rechecks
   the checkout in the same JavaScript operation that fills and clicks, and
   returns `submitted`. The merchant receipt must establish payment success.
   Unknown outcomes cannot replay that approval and require reconciliation.

## Supported scope and trust

- Cards and approvals are tied to the exact checkout origin. Current currencies
  are INR, USD, EUR, GBP, CAD and AUD, all with two minor-unit decimal places.
  The final-total parser is deliberately conservative; it does not claim
  compatibility with any particular real merchant's checkout layout.
- Current fill support requires main-page card fields and one clear final
  button. Hosted payment iframes, wallets, subscriptions and automatic bank/3DS
  completion are not implemented. Bank approval requires owner action.
- Card data is delivered directly over the owned local CDP WebSocket, not through
  a cloud browser task, model tool arguments, Slack, process argv or environment.
  Cloud Browser Tool cards are refused because that provider can log request
  payloads. Login routing prefers the local supervisor when one is active.
- The guarded card release and one-use approval rules are enforced by the
  dedicated payment handlers. Generic browser code is still capable of clicking
  a merchant-saved payment method; instructions prohibit doing that. This is
  not an enforcement boundary against arbitrary malicious agent code or a
  compromised merchant. Browser inspection is not proof of what a merchant's
  backend will charge.
- The gateway/operator host remains trusted. Encryption keys are local beside
  encrypted data. Existing host access, generated-code and profile-isolation
  limitations remain relevant. Temporary encrypted CVV deletion is logical
  cleanup, not a claim of forensic erasure across backups or disk snapshots.
- Removing a card cancels pending owner requests through the existing disconnect
  flow. A saved-card approval validates that the handle still exists and belongs
  to the owner on the captured origin.

## Verification

The canonical Hermes runner passed 117 distinct tests across the payment, hosted-vault,
Browser Tool, cloud browser, native store and native browser-vault suites. The
payment suite covers A → B → A HTTP approval/storage/resume, wrong owner, CSRF,
link replay, expiry, cancellation, changed checkout, wrong task/thread, uncertain
submission and mismatched final totals. The initial six-file run passed 116;
after adding the resumed-purchase `/stop` cancellation case, the two affected
suites passed all 40 tests. Cancellation revokes the temporary CVV before card
release even after the approval has resumed its task.

`verification/probes/clanker_payment_browser_probe.py` passed seven checks with
real sandboxed Chromium and dummy cards: tool discovery and owned endpoint,
first-card submission and receipt, saved-card reuse after fresh HTTP approval,
CVV cleanup, changed-cart refusal, a checkout change between inspection and
write, and foreign-profile refusal. The controlled Example.com DOM replaces the
checkout and generates local dummy receipts. No payment network or real Slack
message is used. Receipt: `verification/evidence/2026-10-06-payment-local-browser.json`.

The local UI fixture at port 8769 shows the actual form and confirmation code.
Approval cleared all inputs and link fragments, hid the form and displayed
Purchase approved. Decline displayed Purchase declined and cleared the form.
Screenshots are under `output/playwright/clanker-payment-*`.

Fresh plugin discovery is verified in temporary profiles. The currently running
Slack gateway predates these handlers; activating them requires a reload after
its active work is accounted for. No live Slack purchase has been performed.

## Files

Implementation: `runtime/vault/payments.py`, the existing vault HTTP/form assets,
and `runtime/seatbelt/plugin.py`. The minimal native store change makes CVV
optional for reusable payment items. Its patch and corresponding native test
are in `patches/hermes/payment-vault.patch`, included by
`scripts/apply-hermes-mods` after the API-key patch.

# Clanker: Composio Browser Tool and the local vault

Active choice: `browser_tool` through the signed-in `itsyyovil@gmail.com` consumer account. Composio CLI 0.4.2 is installed for operator setup; Clanker calls the fixed backend API directly. It never invokes the CLI with a vault password, because the CLI persists tool arguments in local history. No other Composio toolkit is enabled.

The For You billing page stated "No credit card and no subscription." The resolved project is CONSUMER with instant usage disabled. Each runtime session explicitly disables instant usage, workbench, proxy execution, connection management, search and multi-execute, and allows only the five reviewed Browser Tool actions. The response must confirm the browser restrictions and disabled instant usage before any browser task is sent. There is no paid provisioning or automatic switch to a developer project. This does not establish unlimited future free usage.

## Credential path

1. The Slack sender and conversation identify the private Hermes profile. The model supplies a saved vault handle, never an owner or remote browser ID.
2. The backend checks private-DM membership, resolves that handle in that profile's encrypted vault and checks the provider-reported HTTPS page against the saved exact origin.
3. The selected password alone is passed as `secrets={saved_hostname: password}` to CREATE_TASK, along with the saved session ID. The nonsecret account identifier is supplied separately in the fill instructions. The task directs the provider to use the hostname secret only in a password field and stop before submitting. The current login page is preserved when reusing a session; a fresh session starts at the saved exact origin. The password is absent from task text, local state and tool output. Browser Tool and Composio receive that password; the full vault is not uploaded.
4. Provider output is scrubbed against saved secrets and encrypted prior redaction values before returning to Clanker. State and operator keys are in the protected gateway home.

The consumer project's existing log setting is `show_all`; it was not changed. Composio may retain tool arguments, including the selected credential. This handoff is not a claim that provider logging, its internal agent or browser content cannot access secrets. Current host-generated-code permissions also do not independently establish a secrets boundary.

Browser Tool reports the page URL but does not document a CDP/login-field inspection API. Origin checking therefore trusts its URL report; it is weaker than the existing local supervised DOM check. Verification codes now use the private vault's single-use code form and a run-scoped `verification_code` secret. The fill task checks for a visible code field and stops before submission; a wrong origin fails before consuming the code. This path has automated coverage and real Google code entry and sign-in were verified on 2026-10-06. ChatGPT sign-in and CAPTCHA acceptance remain unverified.

## Browser ownership and lifecycle

The initial backend assigned sessions to conversation/profile contexts; it never accepted provider IDs from the model. The 2026-10-06 invitation patch additionally binds new state to workspace, authenticated requester and home, and refuses recorded provider-session ownership collisions. It does not adopt legacy state automatically. A consistent short session name reuses that requester's cookies between completed tasks. Before reuse, the backend checks whether the browser has stopped; an expired browser starts fresh without automatically resending credentials. STOP_TASK stops a task; it does not establish that cookies or the remote browser profile were deleted. Stop now reports profile_retained=null (unknown). Revocation that requires a verified purge remains blocked and reports cleanup pending for this provider. Vault logins remain saved. A missing dispatch acknowledgement blocks automatic retry until an operator reconciles it. A confirmed upstream HTTP 422 body-validation rejection clears that attempt flag, preserves the previous task/session, and returns HTTP 422 without replaying it. The exact upstream HTTP 400 stopped-browser rejection also releases the failed attempt and discards its expired browser IDs; other HTTP 400 responses remain unknown.

The service connection belongs to the operator. This POC does not give each Slack member a separately authorized Composio account. A live synthetic cookie A→B→A test observed an empty fresh B browser and A's cookie on reuse of A; this is evidence for the exercised sessions, not a production tenant-isolation guarantee.

## Verification on 2026-10-05

- 48 focused tests passed after the rejection, browser-expiry and verification-code fixes: Browser Tool and Browser Use adapters, encrypted vault behavior, ownership checks and Slack membership.
- Native Hermes profile discovery A→B→A exposed three browser wrappers, four private-access tools and terminal; no other Composio tools.
- The real consumer API ran a read-only example.com task and the synthetic cookie test with instant billing disabled. Test browsers were stopped afterward.
- A live public demo login passed through the encrypted native vault and Browser Tool, including credential fill and a separate login submission. The demo browser was stopped afterward.
- A Google-only test ran through the existing private Clanker DM and selected native vault login. Browser Tool reported a wrong-password response after submission, so Google sign-in is not verified. A network outage interrupted the Slack agent response, and the cloud browser subsequently stopped. Its exact upstream rejection was reconciled before starting another attempt. A fresh browser reached normal password entry, and Clanker sent a fresh private login form. The original free vault tunnel had expired, so the form could not load. A replacement HTTPS tunnel is running, with a pending local configuration; Slack app-owner access is required to register its callback before activation. The owner sign-in page is open for the user. No account recovery or password reset was completed.
- No paid signup, purchase, commit or publication was performed.

Sources: [Browser Tool schema](https://docs.composio.dev/toolkits/browser_tool), [consumer project authentication](https://docs.composio.dev/docs/consumer-agents), [session restrictions and instant billing](https://docs.composio.dev/reference/api-reference/tool-router/postToolRouterSession), [tool log payloads](https://docs.composio.dev/reference/api-reference/logs).

## Password-fill rejection repair

The real Google fill on 2026-10-05 was rejected by Browser Use V2 before task creation: HTTP 422, `body.secrets`, because the key included `https://`. Composio's public schema advertises URL keys, but its hosted action passes them directly to the V2 endpoint, whose validator accepts hostname characters. The adapter now uses the bare saved hostname and preserves the already inspected login page. Classified input rejections do not strand a session behind the unknown-outcome lock; network failures and ambiguous responses still do.

The existing Google request was not automatically replayed. Its confirmed rejection is reconciled separately against the provider log and the saved session. No Google password reset is required.

## Password-only field repair on 2026-10-06

The latest real Google fill used an input action with `<secret>accounts.google.com</secret>` directly in the password field. That secret held the whole `identifier:password` string. The masked screenshot contained exactly as many password dots as that combined string, rather than the saved password. Google subsequently showed Wrong password. This was a field-binding defect, not evidence that the newly saved password was invalid.

The adapter now sends only the password under the hostname key and supplies the account identifier separately. It encrypts the full supplied secret for output redaction, including passwords containing colons. The field-substitution regression and the existing ownership, vault, lifecycle and membership checks passed: 51 focused tests. Gateway PID 56183 is running the fix. The replacement vault callback and yyovil Slack OIDC are verified. A new Slack test pauses after filling for inspection before Google submission.

The corrected Google submission advanced to the existing phone-number verification challenge (suffix 42). The password was accepted, but full sign-in still requires the owner’s verification. The provider live session is open in Aside for that private step; no account recovery, password reset, or Gmail action was performed.

Live Google verification-code handoff is now exercised: the owner submitted the SMS code in the private vault form, the task resumed automatically, the single-use encrypted payload was consumed, and Browser Tool filled and submitted it. Google advanced to a Redmi 10 Power notification challenge (number 60). Full sign-in remains pending that owner action; no code or password value is stored in repository evidence.

## Final Google E2E acceptance on 2026-10-06

After owner device approval, Clanker’s account inspection and the provider screenshot both confirmed the signed-in Google Account email itsyyovil@gmail.com. The exercised flow passed: Slack private request, encrypted vault password, Browser Tool password fill, private SMS-code form, automatic resume, code submission, device approval, and final account verification. The 51 focused checks also passed. No Gmail, ChatGPT signup, recovery, reset, purchase, commit, or publication action was performed.

Clanker called STOP_TASK after verification. The prior claim that this removed cookies (profile_retained=false) was not supported by a cookie-deletion receipt and has been corrected. The encrypted vault password remains available. The earlier pending callback, SMS, and device-challenge notes above describe resolved test phases. Runtime result_verified remains false for provider reports alone; this acceptance additionally uses operator screenshot review and the owner’s confirmation. It does not establish cross-requester account authorization. See the [invitation and isolation limits](2026-10-06-vault-invitations.md).
# Slack task acknowledgements

Date: 6 October 2026 (Asia/Kolkata). Implementation and local verification are complete. The user approved the installed Slack permission change, and the local gateway was activated at 01:50 IST.

Clanker acknowledges an admitted human message with a reaction selected by the configured model, then keeps Slack's native working indicator active during the task. The reaction is a receipt and stays after completion. Task outcomes are communicated in the reply. Commands, bot posts, synthetic reaction triggers and rejected messages do not receive the new acknowledgement.

The separate classifier receives only the current message, capped at 4,000 characters, under the message's routed profile scope. Its output must be one of `thumbsup`, `eyes`, `wave`, `heart`, `pray`, `raised_hands`, or `muscle`. A four-second timeout, unavailable model or invalid output falls back to neutral `eyes`. The call uses the existing auxiliary router and does not change the main conversation prompt or history. The existing typing refresh starts before selection, so work is visible while the reaction is being selected.

Interim messages preserve processing status and cannot seal a native response stream. Final replies and existing failure/cancellation cleanup clear the indicator. The opt-in default is off for stock Hermes deployments. Existing Clanker profile defaults already disable dynamic per-tool status phrases.

## Configuration

Merge these fields into the shared Slack adapter configuration. Remove the old explicit `typing_status_text: is typing...` so the modern `processing`/`active` API renders Slack's native working label.

```yaml
platforms:
  slack:
    typing_indicator: true
    extra:
      reactions: true
      acknowledgement_reactions: true
```

An optional `auxiliary.slack_acknowledgement` block can select a different provider/model through Hermes's existing auxiliary routing. The current Clanker model works after correcting the Codex auxiliary pool's model selection: a stored cooldown for a different model previously made every model appear unavailable. Known Codex models now respect only their own cooldown, preserving credential-wide limits.

## Verification and activation

Two behavior tests cover six Slack cases using the real auxiliary router and Slack SDK over loopback HTTP: A→B→A credential routing, duplicate-start handling, persistent receipts, status refresh, interim/final delivery, model failure, timeout, invalid output and disallowed completion emojis. A separate real credential-pool test reproduces the Codex selection bug before the fix and verifies both allowed and blocked models afterward. Existing Slack and queued-follow-up checks also pass.

Live model checks returned `thumbsup` for an ordinary task (3.613s), `wave` for a greeting (2.916s), and the neutral fallback for a sensitive message that exceeded four seconds. These checks made no Slack posts or reactions.

The checked-in manifest requests `reactions:write`. Slack's [reaction method](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/reactions.add/) requires that scope; its [status method](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/agents.sessions.setStatus/) uses lifecycle status values. After the user's explicit approval, only that bot scope was added at [Clanker OAuth & Permissions](https://app.slack.com/app-settings/T0C6J1XCDE0/A0C78PBUKQQ/oauth), and the app was reinstalled to the existing `T0C6J1XCDE0` workspace. The existing bot token's live `auth.test` scope header now includes both `reactions:write` and `assistant:write`. No token replacement was needed.

The latest root configuration was backed up and merged with the four UX settings above, with the old custom typing text removed. A semantic comparison confirmed all other configuration values stayed the same. The real gateway configuration loader confirmed the new values. Immediately before replacement, the gateway had zero active agents and no active work. Gateway PID `63285` replaced `56183`, connected to Slack, and retained all five served profiles. The prior gateway exited cleanly; restart notifications remain disabled.

Activation receipts are under `.local/slack-ack-20261006/`: `installed-scope.json`, `config-activation.json`, and the pre/post gateway snapshots. Live rendered acknowledgement/status behavior on a fresh human task remains unobserved; transport tests and installed scopes do not establish visual acceptance.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Invoke the project-versioned Hermes source with dedicated local state.
# The gateway is trusted; enabled generated-code tools use the Seatbelt provider.
set -euo pipefail
umask 077

project_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
lab_dir="$project_dir/.local/hermes-lab"
source_dir="$project_dir/hermes"

if [[ ! -x "$lab_dir/venv/bin/hermes" ]]; then
  echo "Install the pinned baseline first; see verification/LOCAL_BASELINE.md." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if [[ ! -f "$source_dir/pyproject.toml" ]]; then
  echo "Hermes source is missing; expected hermes/ at the project root." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if [[ -e "$source_dir/.env" ]]; then
  echo "The Hermes source has a fallback .env; keep credentials only in the lab home." >&2
  exit 1
fi

mkdir -p "$lab_dir/home" "$lab_dir/workspace" "$lab_dir/gateway-locks" "$lab_dir/managed"
if [[ ! -f "$lab_dir/home/config.yaml" ]]; then
  cp "$project_dir/verification/hermes/config.yaml" "$lab_dir/home/config.yaml"
fi
if [[ ! -f "$lab_dir/home/.env" ]]; then
  touch "$lab_dir/home/.env"
fi
chmod 600 "$lab_dir/home/.env"
if [[ -f "$lab_dir/home/.clanker-execution/fleet.json" ]]; then
  if ! env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH="/usr/bin:/bin" \
      "$lab_dir/venv/bin/python" "$project_dir/runtime/seatbelt/recover.py" "$lab_dir/home"; then
    echo "Browser execution is unavailable; continuing with Slack chat." >&2
  fi
fi

cd "$lab_dir/workspace"
# Credentials must be deliberately configured in the lab home. Keep HOME
# unchanged for platform compatibility; do not inherit provider/session vars.
# Command smoke: skip startup model/tool warmup until inference is configured.
exec env -i \
  HOME="$HOME" \
  PATH="$lab_dir/venv/bin:$lab_dir/home/node/bin:$lab_dir/home/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin" \
  TERM="${TERM:-xterm-256color}" \
  LANG="${LANG:-en_US.UTF-8}" \
  HERMES_HOME="$lab_dir/home" \
  PYTHONPATH="$project_dir/runtime" \
  HERMES_MANAGED_DIR="$lab_dir/managed" \
  HERMES_GATEWAY_LOCK_DIR="$lab_dir/gateway-locks" \
  HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS=1 \
  HERMES_STARTUP_WARMUP_TIMEOUT=0 \
  "$lab_dir/venv/bin/hermes" "$@"
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Apply the clanker modifications only to the audited Hermes pin."""
from pathlib import Path
import hashlib
import json
import shutil
import subprocess

root = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
upstream = root / 'hermes'
pin = 'f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f'
patches = [root / 'patches/hermes/slack-workspace-membership.patch', root / 'patches/hermes/nat64-url-safety.patch', root / 'patches/hermes/slack-unfurl-admission-race.patch', root / 'patches/hermes/hosted-vault.patch', root / 'patches/hermes/api-key-vault.patch', root / 'patches/hermes/payment-vault.patch', root / 'patches/hermes/slack-typing-lifecycle.patch', root / 'patches/hermes/quiet-onboarding.patch', root / 'patches/hermes/slack-acknowledgement.patch', root / 'patches/hermes/codex-auxiliary-model-cooldown.patch']
baseline = json.loads((root / 'verification/hermes/baseline.json').read_text())
if baseline['commit'] != pin or hashlib.sha256((upstream / 'uv.lock').read_bytes()).hexdigest() != baseline['uv_lock_sha256']:
    raise SystemExit('Hermes pin differs; review/rebase the patch before applying.')
for patch in patches:
    check = subprocess.run(['git', 'apply', '--check', str(patch)], cwd=root, capture_output=True)
    if check.returncode == 0:
        subprocess.run(['git', 'apply', str(patch)], cwd=root, check=True)
    else:
        reverse = subprocess.run(['git', 'apply', '--reverse', '--check', str(patch)], cwd=root, capture_output=True)
        if reverse.returncode:
            raise SystemExit('Upstream has conflicting edits; refusing to overwrite them: ' + str(patch))
for source, destination in [
    (root / 'runtime/slack_workspace.py', upstream / 'gateway/slack_workspace.py'),
    (root / 'verification/probes/test_slack_workspace_membership.py', upstream / 'tests/gateway/test_slack_workspace_membership.py'),
]:
    if destination.exists() and destination.read_bytes() != source.read_bytes():
        raise SystemExit(f'{destination} differs; review it before replacing.')
    shutil.copy2(source, destination)
print('Clanker membership, browser, hosted credential/payment vault, Slack acknowledgement/status, auxiliary model and quiet onboarding mods applied to the pinned Hermes checkout.')

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Invoke the project-versioned Hermes source with dedicated local state.
# The gateway is trusted; enabled generated-code tools use the Seatbelt provider.
set -euo pipefail
umask 077

project_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
lab_dir="$project_dir/.local/hermes-lab"
source_dir="$project_dir/hermes"

if [[ ! -x "$lab_dir/venv/bin/hermes" ]]; then
  echo "Install the pinned baseline first; see verification/LOCAL_BASELINE.md." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if [[ ! -f "$source_dir/pyproject.toml" ]]; then
  echo "Hermes source is missing; expected hermes/ at the project root." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if [[ -e "$source_dir/.env" ]]; then
  echo "The Hermes source has a fallback .env; keep credentials only in the lab home." >&2
  exit 1
fi

mkdir -p "$lab_dir/home" "$lab_dir/workspace" "$lab_dir/gateway-locks" "$lab_dir/managed"
if [[ ! -f "$lab_dir/home/config.yaml" ]]; then
  cp "$project_dir/verification/hermes/config.yaml" "$lab_dir/home/config.yaml"
fi
if [[ ! -f "$lab_dir/home/.env" ]]; then
  touch "$lab_dir/home/.env"
fi
chmod 600 "$lab_dir/home/.env"
if [[ -f "$lab_dir/home/.clanker-execution/fleet.json" ]]; then
  if ! env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH="/usr/bin:/bin" \
      "$lab_dir/venv/bin/python" "$project_dir/runtime/seatbelt/recover.py" "$lab_dir/home"; then
    echo "Browser execution is unavailable; continuing with Slack chat." >&2
  fi
fi

cd "$lab_dir/workspace"
# Credentials must be deliberately configured in the lab home. Keep HOME
# unchanged for platform compatibility; do not inherit provider/session vars.
# Command smoke: skip startup model/tool warmup until inference is configured.
exec env -i \
  HOME="$HOME" \
  PATH="$lab_dir/venv/bin:$lab_dir/home/node/bin:$lab_dir/home/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin" \
  TERM="${TERM:-xterm-256color}" \
  LANG="${LANG:-en_US.UTF-8}" \
  HERMES_HOME="$lab_dir/home" \
  PYTHONPATH="$project_dir/runtime" \
  HERMES_MANAGED_DIR="$lab_dir/managed" \
  HERMES_GATEWAY_LOCK_DIR="$lab_dir/gateway-locks" \
  HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS=1 \
  HERMES_STARTUP_WARMUP_TIMEOUT=0 \
  "$lab_dir/venv/bin/hermes" "$@"

The Hermes source is versioned directly in yyot. ## Reproduce a fresh installation

Run from the project root with Git and uv available. A yyot checkout already includes the Hermes source; do not clone over it:

```sh
mkdir -p .local/hermes-lab
test -f hermes/pyproject.toml
test -f hermes/uv.lock
```

Then install the committed dependency selection into its dedicated environment:

```sh
(
  cd hermes
  UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT="$PWD/../.local/hermes-lab/venv" \
    uv sync --locked --python 3.13.13 --extra slack --extra dev
)
ln -s ../.local/hermes-lab/venv hermes/.venv
scripts/hermes-lab --version
```

The symlink ensures the upstream test runner selects this environment before any existing personal Hermes installation. These are fresh-install commands; reuse an existing matching environment. The launcher copies [the initial configuration](hermes/config.yaml) only when the lab has no configuration. **This is configuration separation, not an OS security boundary.** The process keeps the current user's filesystem permissions. Do not use real private accounts for the two-user boundary tests. A functioning container/VM or another verified execution boundary is needed before accepting runtime isolation. Docker's CLI exists on this machine, but its daemon was unavailable at setup time.

## Permission boundary

Slack OIDC establishes the owner of the vault web session. Owner and workspace
come from that session, never request-body fields. CSRF and exact-origin checks
cover invite and revoke. Only native items in that owner's vault can be invited;
guests cannot pass an invited handle to create another invitation.

A durable grant binds workspace, owner, recipient and selected credential.
Saving a member's checklist validates the entire selection and applies all
permission additions/removals in one database transaction. Invalid or foreign
items cause no partial changes. Still-selected credentials retain their grant
handles; unchecked credentials and their pending approvals are revoked before
browser cleanup. Selecting credentials grants no wildcard access to the vault.
Its identity binding includes kind, origin, account identifier and creation
time. The runtime resolves that grant for the authenticated requesting member,
checks current membership of both parties, and verifies the selected native item
still exists with that binding. An unrelated native handle, another member's
grant, a removed or changed account, or a disabled member is denied. Reinvitation
after revocation produces a new grant handle.

These are credential-use permissions. A login can provide the full website
account access available to that login; an API key can provide the permissions
the service gives that key. The implementation does not impose a new read-only
role inside either service. Preventing onward grants is an application rule;
it is not a guarantee that an authorized recipient cannot copy account data or
that a third-party browser provider cannot access an entered credential.

## Execution

Logins fill the requester's supervised local browser, after exact origin and
supported-field inspection. The selected owner password is supplied by the
trusted backend, without switching the active Hermes home to the owner. Owner
TOTP or a hosted owner-only code form can satisfy verification. The one-use code
is consumed in the original requester's task, and automatic resume retains that
requester's source, home and DM.

API requests use `clanker_api_request`: the backend adds the owned or invited key
to a supported authentication header. Calls accept relative paths on the saved
HTTPS origin, reject authentication/Host/Cookie overrides, reject private or
local DNS addresses, pin the connection to a resolved public IP, and verify TLS
against the original hostname. Redirects do not forward authentication. Request
and response sizes are limited. Key values are registered for redaction and
scrubbed from responses. Synthetic transport tests verify these restrictions;
no real external API operation was performed for this change.

Cards use only the requester's supervised local checkout. An invitation lets
the member request a purchase; each exact purchase still needs the **card
owner's** hosted approval and current CVV. The owner sees merchant, order, total,
checkout text and requester. Approval does not transfer the task to the owner.
The handler rechecks the original browser, task, conversation and checkout,
consumes approval and CVV before fill/submission, and refuses replay. Submitted
is not paid; the merchant receipt must be checked. Unsupported payment frames,
wallets, subscriptions and bank approval retain their existing limits.

## Revocation and cookies

Revocation is committed before cleanup and cancels pending delegated code/card
approvals. Secret-bearing browser use is recorded before handoff, with an atomic
active-grant check. This covers a revoke racing between handle resolution and
the usage record. Work already in flight may finish before interruption; the
implementation cannot undo earlier disclosures or completed external actions.

For local Chromium, revoke interrupts the original requester task, closes their
private browsers and deletes their Chromium cookie profile under the guest
execution lock. Cleanup conservatively removes all of that recipient's private
browser state, including sessions used for other valid grants. It preserves the
owner's browser and native vault. An active grant can be used again in a fresh
guest browser after cleanup. API requests have no reusable browser cookies.

If cleanup fails, the grant remains revoked and the recorded usage keeps future
browser/terminal execution blocked. The web UI shows **cleanup pending** and
offers retry. **People with access** also exposes orphan invitations whose
native credential was removed, so that member's access can still be removed or
cleanup retried.

Consumer Browser Tool exposes task stop but no reviewed cookie/session deletion
operation. Its stop result now reports `profile_retained: null` (unknown),
correcting the previous unsupported claim of cookie deletion. A required purge
stops the task, keeps a blocked tombstone, and returns cleanup pending. Repeated
stop/retry does not clear that block. Operator cleanup needs an actual provider
deletion/reconciliation capability before a verified reset can be recorded;
this implementation does not supply that capability.

## Browser routing and unresolved incident work

New cloud state keys include workspace, authenticated requester and resolved
home, independent of the short session name or a shared conversation profile.
State carries an explicit owner marker. Provider session IDs are recorded with
that owner/context, and a recorded collision is refused and quarantined. Legacy
state is not silently adopted by the new namespace. Unknown dispatch outcomes
retain their retry block.

These controls govern Clanker's assignments and known grants. They do not prove
a fresh remote browser lacks another account's pre-existing cookies. Provider
ownership collisions are detected on acknowledgement, after task dispatch;
that check cannot undo observations the provider made before acknowledging.
Free-form remote task instructions are not an account-authorization boundary.
The reported disclosure therefore still requires tracing and invalidating
affected legacy/provider state, a provider-enforced requester isolation and
pre-read authorization design, and real two-requester/DM-handoff acceptance.
Existing login state alone must never be used as permission.

# Owner-approved payment cards in the local POC

Clanker can collect a card in the private vault form, save the reusable number,
expiry and optional cardholder name, and use it in a particular checkout after
the owner approves that purchase. This implementation is local POC code. Real
merchant payment acceptance, production hosting and payment compliance have not
been verified.

## Flow

1. Prepare a one-time card checkout with `browser_exec` in the owner's private
   local browser. `clanker_request_payment` takes its exact `checkout_url`, the
   merchant, item/quantity/delivery summary, final `amount_minor` including fees,
   currency, and an optional saved-card handle.
2. The backend checks that the browser endpoint belongs to that profile, finds
   the exact checkout tab, and captures its origin, URL, visible contents and one
   visible Pay/Place order button. A recognizable final-total line must match
   the requested amount. Unsupported or ambiguous totals fail before collection.
3. The existing private Slack handoff sends an owner-bound vault link. The same
   Slack OIDC session and CSRF controls protect the form. The owner sees the
   merchant, origin, summary, amount and expandable actual checkout text. Card
   fields are masked. Approval is explicit and specific to one purchase.
4. Saving encrypts reusable card fields in the owner's native Hermes VaultStore.
   CVV is excluded from that item. It is separately encrypted for this approval,
   expires within five minutes, and is cleared on use, cancellation or expiry
   cleanup. Saved-card reuse shows the last four digits and asks for current CVV
   and fresh approval. The approval link expires after fifteen minutes.
5. The task resumes with a request ID, never card values. `clanker_pay` verifies
   owner, profile, task, conversation, exact browser, page contents and stamped
   button. It consumes approval durably before card-bearing browser I/O, rechecks
   the checkout in the same JavaScript operation that fills and clicks, and
   returns `submitted`. The merchant receipt must establish payment success.
   Unknown outcomes cannot replay that approval and require reconciliation.

## Supported scope and trust

- Cards and approvals are tied to the exact checkout origin. Current currencies
  are INR, USD, EUR, GBP, CAD and AUD, all with two minor-unit decimal places.
  The final-total parser is deliberately conservative; it does not claim
  compatibility with any particular real merchant's checkout layout.
- Current fill support requires main-page card fields and one clear final
  button. Hosted payment iframes, wallets, subscriptions and automatic bank/3DS
  completion are not implemented. Bank approval requires owner action.
- Card data is delivered directly over the owned local CDP WebSocket, not through
  a cloud browser task, model tool arguments, Slack, process argv or environment.
  Cloud Browser Tool cards are refused because that provider can log request
  payloads. Login routing prefers the local supervisor when one is active.
- The guarded card release and one-use approval rules are enforced by the
  dedicated payment handlers. Generic browser code is still capable of clicking
  a merchant-saved payment method; instructions prohibit doing that. This is
  not an enforcement boundary against arbitrary malicious agent code or a
  compromised merchant. Browser inspection is not proof of what a merchant's
  backend will charge.
- The gateway/operator host remains trusted. Encryption keys are local beside
  encrypted data. Existing host access, generated-code and profile-isolation
  limitations remain relevant. Temporary encrypted CVV deletion is logical
  cleanup, not a claim of forensic erasure across backups or disk snapshots.
- Removing a card cancels pending owner requests through the existing disconnect
  flow. A saved-card approval validates that the handle still exists and belongs
  to the owner on the captured origin.

    shutil.copy2(source, destination)

# Task acknowledgement verification

6 October 2026, Asia/Kolkata. Local implementation verified; installed Slack permission change explicitly approved and local gateway activated at 01:50 IST.

## Behavior

The new Slack tests reproduced fixed `eyes` reactions and premature status clearing on the unchanged adapter. With the patch, the real auxiliary router and Slack SDK over loopback HTTP verify model-selected reactions, A→B→A profile credential routing, idempotent start hooks, persistent receipts, and processing status across normal, empty and failed interim sends. Final delivery clears processing. Failure, timeout, malformed output and attempted completion emojis produce a neutral receipt without breaking delivery.

The Codex helper initially reported no credentials despite a populated OAuth pool. The pool correctly treats model-less selection conservatively when any model is cooled down, but the helper had a known model and failed to pass it. A real temporary-pool test failed before the fix and passes afterward for both an unrelated allowed model and the blocked model. Existing pool test doubles were updated to accept the real selector's model keyword.

## Tests

The canonical `scripts/run_tests.sh` runner passed 482 distinct relevant cases across these files:

```text
tests/gateway/test_slack_acknowledgement.py                 6
tests/gateway/test_slack_typing_lifecycle.py                3
tests/gateway/test_slack.py                              211
tests/gateway/test_slack_native_streaming.py               21
tests/gateway/test_slack_require_mention_channels.py         3
tests/gateway/test_slack_workspace_membership.py             6
tests/gateway/test_queued_followup_processing_hooks.py       7
tests/agent/test_auxiliary_codex_pool_model.py               2
tests/agent/test_auxiliary_auto_never_guesses_provider.py    4
tests/agent/test_auxiliary_client_resolve_dedup.py            3
tests/agent/test_auxiliary_client.py                      216
```

One unrelated case in the auxiliary client file requires the absent `anthropic` package and fails while constructing its Anthropic transport. Its diagnostic explicitly reports the missing package. The final auxiliary run excluded only `test_anthropic_messages_profile_resolves_to_messages_adapter`; this is not a fully green unfiltered auxiliary suite. No dependency was installed.

Ruff passes on the three new Python files. `git diff --check` passes for the modified upstream files. `scripts/apply-hermes-mods` is idempotent. A fresh replay of all 10 registered patches against the imported Git index produced all 25 managed files byte-for-byte equal to the current source.

## Live checks and remaining acceptance

The configured model returned `thumbsup` for an ordinary task in 3.613 seconds and `wave` for a greeting in 2.916 seconds. A sensitive prompt exceeded four seconds and correctly fell back to `eyes`. These were classifier-only probes with no Slack message, reaction or status write.

Before approval, Slack's live `auth.test` OAuth header and the app settings lacked `reactions:write`. The checked-in manifest adds only that scope. Following explicit user approval, the scope was saved and Clanker was reinstalled to the existing workspace `T0C6J1XCDE0`. The existing bot token now reports `reactions:write`, `reactions:read` and `assistant:write`; all other installed scopes match the prior snapshot. No token replacement was needed. The safe app-settings screenshot is `.local/slack-ack-20261006/slack-permission-installed.jpg`.

The latest root configuration was backed up before merging `typing_indicator: true`, `extra.reactions: true`, and `extra.acknowledgement_reactions: true`, while removing the old explicit custom typing text. A semantic comparison confirmed no unrelated values changed, and the real `load_gateway_config()` returned the expected values.

Immediately before the approved replacement, gateway PID `56183` had zero active agents and no active work. It exited cleanly. New gateway PID `63285` reported `running`, Slack `connected`, no platform error or attention flag, and the same five served profiles. Restart notifications remain disabled. Machine receipts are `.local/slack-ack-20261006/installed-scope.json`, `config-activation.json`, `gateway.pre-activation.json`, and `gateway.post-activation.json`.

Live rendered acknowledgement/status behavior on a fresh human task remains unobserved. Unit/transport tests, classifier probes, installed scopes and startup health do not establish rendered Slack UI acceptance. No synthetic Slack message was posted for this verification.
